questions.text: A Coronas Type I school requires 6+ ACH for health/wellbeing without mechanical cooling. Calculate whether a 20m × 15m classroom with 4m ceiling (cross-ventilation + stack effect) can achieve this rate, given SW monsoon 3.5 m/s average wind and outdoor–indoor ΔT 2°C.

options.text: Cross-ventilation: Well-designed asymmetric windows (8% inlet, 25% outlet on 60m perimeter) can yield 4–6 ACH in 3.5 m/s wind. Stack effect (4m height, 2°C ΔT): ≈ 0.25 Pa → 2–3 ACH. Combined: 6–9 ACH achievable. With operable partitions enabling multi-zone stack, target is met without mechanical cooling
With ideal geometry, 6 ACH is unachievable in tropical climates; mechanical AC is mandatory for schools
Stack effect is negligible; cross-ventilation alone cannot reach 6 ACH
Wind speed 3.5 m/s is insufficient; 5+ m/s required for 6 ACH

rationale.b: 6 ACH is achievable in tropical Type I climates with design optimization; mechanical cooling is not mandatory for schools.
rationale.c: Stack effect contributes 2–3 ACH; combined with cross-ventilation, the target is reached.
rationale.d: 3.5 m/s is adequate for tropical monsoon; higher wind speeds assist but are not required.
rationale.correct: This tests the synergistic mechanism. tested calculation shows: 'Combined Cross + Stack: 6–12 ACH (synergistic)... Wind Speed Dependency: Varies 2–5 m/s seasonal (Type I).' At 3.5 m/s (within Type I range), cross-ventilation (4–6 ACH) + stack effect (2–3 ACH) combine for 6–9 ACH. The synergy is critical; neither alone suffices, but together they achieve 6+ ACH target for ASHRAE 55 adaptive compliance.
rationale.takeaway: The synergy is critical; neither alone suffices, but together they achieve 6+ ACH target for ASHRAE 55 adaptive compliance.

questions.text: For a Coronas Type II hospital in Manila (no dry season, perpetual low wind, continuous 24/7 occupancy), design a ventilation strategy combining cross-ventilation, stack effect, and supplementary cooling. Justify each mechanism's role.

options.text: Rely solely on mechanical air conditioning; natural ventilation is insufficient in Type II, given the climate's high humidity

Cross-ventilation (primary, 2–3 ACH weak wind): windows on all four sides, multi-zone layout, operable partitions. Stack effect (backup, 2–4 ACH): 6–8m atrium from ground to roof vent provides buoyancy-driven flow 24/7 regardless of wind. Supplementary evaporative cooling (tertiary): desiccant dehumidification for 75% RH exterior → 60% interior, enhancing passive cooling. Hybrid strategy reduces mechanical reliance 30–40%
Natural ventilation cannot achieve occupant comfort; sealed mechanical systems are mandatory to ensure consistent air quality
Type II climate is too wet; evaporative cooling is ineffective, making mechanical systems the only viable option

rationale.a: Mechanical AC can be primary, but natural ventilation provides meaningful backup (30–40% cooling load reduction).
rationale.c: Hybrid design (natural + mechanical) outperforms sealed mechanical alone for both comfort and energy efficiency.
rationale.d: Type II high humidity reduces evaporative cooling benefit, but supplementary dehumidification can enhance passive strategy.
rationale.correct: This is the tested multi-mechanism integration for Type II: 'For Coronas Type II hospital (no dry season, perpetual low wind)... design a ventilation strategy combining cross-ventilation, stack effect, and supplementary evaporative cooling.' case study specifies: 'Combined cross + stack: 6–12 ACH (synergistic); Coronas Type II (year-round weak wind + thermal buoyancy blend) is optimal for atrium stack effect.'
rationale.takeaway: design a ventilation strategy combining cross-ventilation, stack effect, and supplementary evaporative cooling.' case study specifies: 'Combined cross + stack: 6–12 ACH (synergistic); Coronas Type II (year-round weak wind + thermal buoyancy blend) is optimal for atrium stack effect.'.

questions.text: A Coronas Type I office building in Manila requires natural ventilation during both monsoon (May–Oct, SW wind 225°) and calm seasons (Nov–Apr). How must window placement accommodate bidirectional flow?

options.text: Windows on only two perpendicular walls (standard cross-ventilation); seasonal reversal is managed by temporary screens, which are adjusted biannually
Type I has uniform wind direction year-round; single-orientation window placement suffices, assuming no obstructions
Seasonal wind reversal makes natural ventilation impossible; mechanical AC is mandatory unless alternative passive systems are implemented

Windows and doors positioned at multiple compass orientations (not just two); interior doors remain open enabling multi-zone cross-ventilation. Stack effect operates year-round regardless of wind direction, providing backup when seasonal reversals create non-optimal wind exposure

rationale.a: Two-wall orientation cannot accommodate seasonal wind reversal adequately; multi-orientation is necessary.
rationale.b: Type I explicitly has monsoon reversal (SW May–Oct, NE Nov–Apr); wind direction changes seasonally.
rationale.c: Stack effect + multi-oriented windows enable year-round natural ventilation despite seasonal wind reversal; mechanical AC is not mandatory.
rationale.correct: For Coronas Type I climates with seasonal wind reversal, buildings must accommodate bidirectional flow: Windows and doors positioned at multiple compass orientations (not just two). Interior doors between rooms remain open (enables multi-zone cross-ventilation). Stack effect operates regardless of wind direction, providing year-round backup.'
rationale.takeaway: Stack effect operates regardless of wind direction, providing year-round backup.'.

questions.text: What is a 'wind catcher' (windtower) and how does it enhance tropical natural ventilation?

options.text: A window-mounted screen that blocks wind, which is not its intended function

A passive ventilation device that captures air at height (3–8m) above street-level turbulence, channels it down into building via vertical shaft (stack effect amplification), and creates Venturi-effect suction on downwind side. Combined effects drive ventilation 2–3× greater than window-level cross-ventilation
A decorative architectural element with no functional ventilation benefit, which is incorrect
A mechanical fan system requiring electrical power, which contradicts its passive nature

rationale.a: Wind catchers capture and direct wind flow; they do not block it.
rationale.c: Wind catchers have proven passive ventilation function, quantified at 2–3× window-only effectiveness.
rationale.d: Wind catchers are entirely passive; no electrical power required.
rationale.correct: Wind catchers are defined: 'A passive ventilation device that captures air at height and channels it down into a building, exploiting both wind pressure and the Venturi effect. Effectiveness: Coronas Type I excellent during monsoon (May–Oct); less effective in calm dry season.'
rationale.takeaway: Effectiveness: Coronas Type I excellent during monsoon (May–Oct); less effective in calm dry season.'.

questions.text: A wind catcher installation for a Coronas Type I office in Cebu (SW monsoon 225°) should be sized with height 5m above adjacent rooflines and duct diameter 0.8m. Why are these specifications critical for tropical effectiveness?

options.text: Height 5m above surroundings captures wind above street-level turbulence zone (where regional wind dominates). Duct diameter 0.8m creates constriction amplifying Venturi effect. Undersized height (roofline level) eliminates advantage; oversized ducts (>1.0m) reduce velocity. Type I monsoon winds (3–5 m/s average) require this tuning for effectiveness
Tropical wind catchers should be installed at ground level for safety, which contradicts their purpose
Type I seasonal wind variation makes wind catcher unreliable; design for mechanical backup only, which is not the primary design strategy
Height and duct size are irrelevant; wind catchers function equally at roofline level with any duct diameter, which is incorrect

rationale.b: Ground-level installation eliminates height advantage; roofline minimum is 5m ABOVE adjacent structures.
rationale.c: Type I monsoon provides strong seasonal wind (May–Oct); wind catchers are highly effective during this period. Mechanical backup handles calm season (Nov–Apr).
rationale.d: Height and duct sizing are critical to wind catcher functionality; 'critical' is the tested term.
rationale.correct: Minimum height: 5 meters above surrounding buildings (escapes street-level turbulence)... Duct cross-section: 0.5–1.0 m² typical for residential; larger for commercial.' Height advantage and constriction-driven velocity are the core mechanisms. Undersizing either defeats the design.

questions.text: Explain why naturally ventilated buildings can achieve occupant comfort at higher interior temperatures (26–29°C per ASHRAE 55 adaptive model) compared to selead mechanical buildings (23–25°C), and how this understanding changes ventilation design strategy.

options.text: ASHRAE 55 adaptive model recognizes that naturally ventilated occupants adapt physiologically and psychologically to higher temperatures. Variable air movement (0.5–1.5 m/s) and occupant control (opening windows) increase thermal tolerance. Result: 26–29°C with 6+ ACH = same comfort as 23–25°C sealed building. This 3–4K tolerance window enables 35–50% cooling energy savings and justifies investment in passive ventilation design
ASHRAE 55 allows higher temperatures only in non-occupancy periods, which means that during occupied times, temperatures must be maintained at lower levels
Higher temperatures in natural ventilation are unacceptable; sealed buildings always provide better comfort, ensuring consistent thermal conditions
Occupant adaptation reduces comfort; natural ventilation comfort is always lower, leading to potential dissatisfaction among building users

rationale.b: ASHRAE 55 applies continuously; adaptive model is active during all occupancy periods.
rationale.c: Adaptive model legitimizes higher comfort temperatures in naturally ventilated buildings; comfort is not compromised.
rationale.d: Occupant adaptation enhances comfort by enabling personal control and reducing mechanical dependency.
rationale.correct: ASHRAE 55 Adaptive Comfort Model recognizes that naturally ventilated buildings can maintain occupant comfort at higher indoor temperatures (26–29°C) than fully air-conditioned spaces (23–25°C) because: (1) Occupants adapt psychologically and physiologically; (2) Variable air movement and thermal conditions increase engagement; (3) Personal control enhances tolerance.'
rationale.takeaway: ASHRAE 55 Adaptive Comfort Model recognizes that naturally ventilated buildings can maintain occupant comfort at higher indoor temperatures (26–29°C) than fully air-conditioned spaces (23–25°C) because: (1) Occupants adapt psychologically and physiologically; (2) Variable air movement and thermal conditions increase engagement; (3) Personal control enhances tolerance.'.

questions.text: Calculate the stack effect pressure differential for a 6-meter-tall library space (exterior 34°C, interior 37.5°C via passive cooling). Show calculation and estimate resulting ACH contribution.

options.text: ΔP = 1.2 × 9.81 × 4 × (2.5/308) = 0.38 Pa. This modest pressure generates 2–4 ACH in typical rooms. Combined with wind-driven flow (4–8 ACH), stack effect provides crucial backup during low-wind periods
A 6-meter space generates ΔP > 1.0 Pa, driving 8–10 ACH, assuming no obstructions in the airflow path
Height is irrelevant to stack effect; only temperature differential matters, which is a common misconception
Stack effect is negligible in tropical climates; pressure differentials <0.5 Pa are ineffective, especially in well-ventilated spaces

rationale.b: 0.38 Pa is the correct result; this is not >1.0 Pa.
rationale.c: Height (h in formula) directly affects ΔP magnitude; 6m vs. 3m height produces 50% greater pressure differential.
rationale.d: 0.38 Pa, though modest, drives measurable airflow (2–4 ACH); tropical buildings cannot ignore stack effect.
rationale.correct: The exact calculation: 'h = 4 m (ground floor to roof opening), ΔT = 2.5 K, T_ext = 308 K... ΔP = 0.38 Pa... 2–4 air changes per hour.' This modest pressure, while not dominant, provides essential backup when wind is absent. The calculation + ACH estimation is the tested skill.
rationale.takeaway: The calculation + ACH estimation is the tested skill.

questions.text: How do Venturi-shaped roofs differ from flat roofs in their impact on natural ventilation, and when is the additional complexity cost-justified?

options.text: Venturi roofs are universally required for all tropical buildings, regardless of specific site conditions or climate variations
Flat roofs are always superior; Venturi geometry worsens airflow, making them unsuitable for most applications

Venturi-shaped roofs (widest at bottom, narrowest at top) accelerate exhaust air and create suction enhancing stack effect by 15–25%. Cost-justified in Type II/IV (perpetual buoyancy reliance) where year-round 0.5+ Pa additional pressure is valuable. Coronas Type I daytime heating may not justify complexity; simpler flat + roof vents often suffice
Venturi roofs add no functional benefit; complexity is unnecessary, as simpler designs achieve the same results

rationale.a: Universal requirement is overstated; cost-benefit drives application.
rationale.b: Venturi geometry enhances stack effect; it improves, not worsens, airflow.
rationale.d: 15–25% ventilation increase is significant; complexity is justified in low-wind climates.
rationale.correct: Venturi roofs increase ventilation rates by 15–25% compared to flat roofs... In calm wind conditions (<1 m/s), Venturi effect accounts for only 10–15% additional flow; wind-driven flow dominates under favorable conditions.' Cost-benefit analysis determines necessity: Type II perpetual low-wind conditions justify investment; Type I strong monsoon may not require it.
rationale.takeaway: In calm wind conditions (<1 m/s), Venturi effect accounts for only 10–15% additional flow; wind-driven flow dominates under favorable conditions.' Cost-benefit analysis determines necessity: Type II perpetual low-wind conditions justify investment; Type I strong monsoon may not require it.

questions.text: Compare the ventilation effectiveness of well-designed cross-ventilation (VE = 0.7–0.85) versus poorly configured layouts (VE = 0.3–0.5). What design factor primarily drives this difference?

options.text: Window size alone determines ventilation efficiency; larger windows always yield higher VE, regardless of their placement or orientation within the building envelope
Climate type determines VE; Type I is always more efficient than Type II, due to inherent differences in temperature and humidity levels that affect air movement

Ventilation efficiency depends on clear flow paths between openings, interior partitions (obstructions), and window positioning. Well-designed open floor plans achieve VE 0.7–0.85 (most air reaches occupied zones). Poorly partitioned buildings waste ventilation volume in dead zones; same air volume provides only 30–50% occupant benefit
Ventilation efficiency is constant regardless of interior layout, as long as the total window area meets the minimum code requirements for natural ventilation

rationale.a: Window size is one factor, but layout (partitions, flow paths) is equally critical.
rationale.b: Both Type I and Type II can achieve high or low VE depending on layout; climate does not determine efficiency.
rationale.d: Layout directly affects VE; design choices matter greatly.
rationale.correct: : 'Ventilation efficiency (VE) = Volume of fresh air reaching breathing zone / Total ventilation rate... Well-designed cross-ventilation: VE = 0.7–0.85... Poorly configured layouts: VE = 0.3–0.5.' The difference is layout quality—open floor plans enable high VE; partitions block flow and waste air volume.
rationale.takeaway: Poorly configured layouts: VE = 0.3–0.5.' The difference is layout quality—open floor plans enable high VE; partitions block flow and waste air volume.

questions.text: What are the two primary driving forces for natural ventilation in tropical buildings?

options.text: Pressure-driven flow (wind) and buoyancy-driven flow (stack effect); both are perpetual in Philippine climate
Humidity and rainfall patterns, which significantly influence ventilation needs and strategies
Mechanical fans and window operation, which are often used in conjunction with natural ventilation methods
Solar radiation intensity and building height, which can affect air movement and ventilation effectiveness

rationale.b: Humidity and rainfall affect moisture management but not ventilation mechanics.
rationale.c: Mechanical systems are active, not natural ventilation.
rationale.d: These affect thermal conditions but are not primary ventilation drivers.
rationale.correct: Natural ventilation operates through two primary mechanisms: pressure-driven flow (wind) and buoyancy-driven flow (stack effect). Both are perpetual in the Philippine climate; their interaction determines achievable ventilation rates.'
rationale.takeaway: Both are perpetual in the Philippine climate; their interaction determines achievable ventilation rates.'.

questions.text: Explain why asymmetric aperture sizing (small inlet 6–10% floor area, large outlet 20–30%) is more effective than symmetric equal-sized openings for cross-ventilation in tropical buildings.

options.text: Asymmetry reduces daylighting; symmetric windows are better for interior illumination, which is crucial for energy efficiency and occupant comfort
Small inlets reduce occupant comfort; large outlets are preferable, as they allow for greater airflow and temperature regulation

Asymmetric sizing creates velocity at small inlet (Bernoulli effect: fluid accelerates through constriction), amplifying pressure differential. Large outlet prevents backflow/pressure buildup. Result: higher air velocity, greater penetration depth into building interior. Symmetric 18%+18% openings yield lower velocity and shallower penetration; asymmetric 6%+28% is 20–30% more effective
Symmetric sizing is universally optimal; asymmetry has no advantage, as it complicates design without providing significant benefits

rationale.a: Outlet size (20–30%) can be high-placement louvers (roof vents) that do not impact daylighting; asymmetry and lighting are independent.
rationale.b: Small inlets (6–10%) are high-velocity air, which occupants perceive as refreshing; comfort is enhanced, not reduced.
rationale.d: Asymmetry is demonstrably more effective; this is tested design knowledge.
rationale.correct: Aperture sizing is counterintuitive. Smaller inlet openings (6–10% of floor area) create velocity; larger outlets (20–30% of floor area) maximize volume. Asymmetric aperture sizing is more effective than equal-sized openings.' This applies Bernoulli principle: constriction creates speed, preventing backflow.
rationale.takeaway: Asymmetric aperture sizing is more effective than equal-sized openings.' This applies Bernoulli principle: constriction creates speed, preventing backflow.
